He surveyed the little volume with an air of theatrical gravity. “A gift of such peculiar elegance, Miss Croft, must surely be the source of great satisfaction. I imagine your benefactor in London takes some pleasure in picturing your delight. Does he, I wonder, guess that the book arrived this very Tuesday? Or was his order a more general one, a matter of convenience for the bookseller, with no precise day in mind?” He tilted his head, his eyes full of a mischief that Eleanor found both vexing and diverting.

Catherine Croft, who had been diligently applying herself to her needlework, looked up, her colour a little heightened. “You give Mr. Green too much credit for elaborate schemes, Mr. Audley. I believe he recalled I had a fondness for Italian poetry, and acted upon it. Nothing more.”

“Nothing more! Ah, but the simplest acts are often the most profound. ‘A fondness for Italian poetry.’ It is a very specific fondness, is it not? And to remember it, and to act upon it with such taste—Petrarch! and in such a very fine binding. It speaks of a most particular and constant regard.” He turned a page with a delicate touch. “I should not be surprised if a letter were to follow shortly, inquiring anxiously after its reception.”

Eleanor could not forbear a small smile at Miss Croft’s evident discomfort, though she felt a pang of conscience for it. This poor, quiet girl was no match for Mr. Audley’s playful persecution. She caught his eye and gave him a slight, reproving shake of the head, but he only smiled the more.

“Indeed, one might conjecture a great deal,” he continued, half to Eleanor, half to the room at large. “One might conjecture, for instance, that this sonnet here—‘*L’aura serena che fra verdi fronde*’—was a particular favourite. There, the bookmark is placed just so. A happy accident, perhaps, or a gentle hint?”

He was interrupted by the return of Catherine’s aunt, Mrs. Finch, who entered from the garden with a small basket of withered blooms. “Oh! Mr. Audley, you have the book! Is it not a treasure? So very kind of Mr. Green. I must remember to thank his sister when next I see her for the receipt for the preserved damsons; they were a triumph, an absolute triumph. Catherine, my dear, you have not offered our guests any refreshment. We have some ratafia cakes, Eleanor, that I think you will like. Poor Catherine has been so overwhelmed with this excitement, she has forgot all her duties!”

“We have been perfectly well entertained, I assure you, ma’am,” said Eleanor, rising to help the older woman.

“I have been admiring the volume,” said Mr. Audley, closing it at last. “Miss Croft and I were just conjecturing as to the sender’s motives.”

“Oh, there is no conjecture about it!” cried Mrs. Finch, setting her basket down with a thump. “Mr. Green has always been a friend to the family. When my late husband was ill, he was so very attentive; he would send over the papers every other day. Though I confess I thought this book might have come from young Mr. Bellamy, in town for his studies. He was so very struck with Catherine at the winter assembly, you know. He quite stared at her. Did you not notice, Catherine? You were wearing your blue muslin. But no, the man from the bookseller said Mr. Green’s name quite distinctly. It is a puzzle, to be sure.”

Mr. Audley exchanged a look with Eleanor of pure amusement. “A puzzle indeed, madam. Life is full of them.” He walked over to the window where a gentleman, Mr. Davies, had been standing in quiet observation of the proceedings. “Davies, you are very silent. Have you no theory to offer on the subject of mysterious gifts?”

Mr. Davies turned, his expression mild and unreadable. “I have ever found that the pleasure of a gift is in the receiving of it,” he said, his gaze resting for a moment on Miss Croft, “not in the ceaseless examination of its origins. I was admiring Mrs. Finch’s roses. They have survived the last frost better than ours at the Grange.”

His gentle rebuke was not lost on Eleanor, who felt her cheeks grow warm. Mr. Audley, however, was impervious. “A practical man, as always! While we are unravelling the threads of human sentiment, you are considering the frost. And yet,” he added, moving back towards the centre of the room, “I cannot help but return to it. This Mr. Green or Mr. Bellamy—he has excellent taste in music too, I collect?”

Catherine looked at him, bewildered. “Music, sir? I do not understand you.”

“Why, this bookmark,” said he, reopening the Petrarch and plucking a thin ribbon of silk from its pages. “It is not a bookmark at all. It is from a Clementi sonatina, I believe; the one you played at the vicarage last month. See, here are the bars. A curious thing to find in a book of Italian poetry sent from London, is it not? Unless the sender had heard you play it, and wished to remind you.”

He held the ribbon out. For a moment, no one spoke. Catherine Croft stared at the scrap of music as if it were a serpent, her face entirely drained of colour. She put her hand to her throat.

Eleanor spoke quickly, to cover the dreadful silence. “What a singular coincidence! I suppose such ribbons are used for all manner of things.”

“I suppose they are,” said Mr. Audley, his smile finally fading as he perceived the genuine distress he had caused. “It is nonsense, of course. Forgive me, Miss Croft. I am talking nonsense.”

But the damage was done. The easy atmosphere of the visit had been shattered. Mrs. Finch began a rambling story about a time she had found a fish hook in a library book, and under the cover of this diversion, Eleanor and Mr. Audley soon took their leave.

As they walked towards the lane, he was uncharacteristically quiet. At last, Eleanor said, “You went too far, Mr. Audley.”

“Yes,” he said, with a sigh. “I believe I did. I had no idea—I thought she was merely coquetting. I thought she enjoyed the mystery.”

“You thought she was a character in a play of your own devising,” replied Eleanor, with more severity than she had intended. “But she is a person, and I believe, a person with a secret she is not at liberty to share. That ribbon was no coincidence. And the book, I fancy, came neither from Mr. Green nor Mr. Bellamy.” She glanced at him. “You know something of this.”

He did not deny it. He only said, “I know that I have been a fool. And I have made a muddle of a very delicate business.” And for the rest of the walk to her father’s gate, he said not another word, leaving Eleanor to conjecture, with a great deal more anxiety than amusement, on what that delicate business might be.

Mr. Audley’s admission of folly, so frankly given, did little to soothe her. It served only to confirm that the matter was indeed as delicate as he claimed, and that his own part in it, whatever that might be, had been one of inexcusable levity. Her vexation with him was profound; it was a vexation born not only of his exposing poor Catherine to such public mortification, but of the disappointment she felt in him. She had thought him possessed of a finer sensibility, a judgment that, however playful, would never stray into cruelty. To have been so mistaken was a blow to her own discernment.

At her father’s gate, he stopped and turned to her, his countenance for once entirely stripped of its usual lively irony. “Miss Leigh,” he said, his voice low, “I cannot hope that you will think well of me after this morning’s work. I can only assure you that my intentions, foolish as my conduct has been, were not malicious. I have been meddling where I ought to have shown the greatest forbearance.”

“Forbearance would certainly have been preferable to what you did shew, Mr. Audley,” she replied, her tone colder than she had intended. “Miss Croft’s feelings are not a game to be played for the amusement of the company.”

“You are right. You are perfectly right,” he answered, without any attempt at self-defence. “I have behaved abominably. Will you permit me to call upon your father tomorrow? There is something I believe I ought to explain, if you would be so good as to hear me.”

Eleanor considered this. Her curiosity was certainly a powerful advocate in his favour, but her sense of propriety, and her loyalty to the distressed Catherine, argued against it. “I am not certain that it is my place to hear any explanation, sir. The apology is surely owed to Miss Croft, not to me.”

“And it shall be made, I promise you. But my offense against her was one of ignorance, while my offense against you, and against the better judgment I hoped you credited me with, was one of character. It is that which I would, if I could, attempt to repair.” He looked at her with such genuine contrition that her resolve began to soften. He was a fool, perhaps, but he was a repentant one. After a moment’s hesitation, she gave a slight nod. “My father and I will be at home tomorrow morning.” He bowed, his gratitude evident in the gesture, and without another word, he turned and walked back down the lane, leaving Eleanor to proceed into the house with a mind even more agitated than before.

She found her father in his library, surrounded by the comfortable clutter of books and maps that was his natural element. Mr. Leigh was a gentleman of quiet habits and a discerning mind, whose affection for his daughter was the chief business of his life. He looked up from a letter as she entered.

“Ah, Eleanor, my dear. You have been gone some time. Was your visit to Mrs. Finch a pleasant one?”

“It was…eventful, Papa,” she said, removing her bonnet and sitting in the chair opposite him. She was in no mood to be reticent; her father’s steady sense was the very tonic she required. She related the whole of the morning’s occurrences, from the arrival of the Petrarch to the unfortunate discovery of the musical ribbon, and Mr. Audley’s relentless, targeted teasing. She did not spare Mr. Audley, but she tried to be just, including his final expression of regret and his desire to call upon them to explain himself.

Mr. Leigh listened with his customary attentiveness, his fingers steepled before him. When she had finished, he was silent for a moment. “Poor Miss Croft,” he said at last. “It is a hard thing for a young woman to have her private sentiments held up to public scrutiny. And Mr. Audley has shown a want of consideration that is, I must own, surprising in a man of his understanding.”

His error was in making a jest of what is clearly a matter of great anxiety to the poor girl.”

Eleanor felt a pang of apprehension on Catherine’s behalf. To be obliged to sit through a dinner, making conversation with a suitor approved by her parents, while her heart was secretly engaged elsewhere, seemed a particular form of torment. Her father, however, insisted they must go. “We cannot shut ourselves up, my dear,” he had said. “And it will not do for Miss Croft to be seen to be hiding. She must brazen it out.”

Catherine Croft looked pale and drawn, though she was making a visible effort to appear cheerful. Mr. Harris, a solid, sensible-looking man of about thirty with a florid complexion and an air of unshakeable self-worth, was seated near her, discoursing on the price of wool. Mrs. Finch was already in the midst of a complicated anecdote about a lost thimble. The only surprise was the final guest to be announced, just as the vicar’s wife was despairing of his arrival: Mr. Audley.

He entered the room with an apology for his lateness, blaming a lame horse. His eyes immediately sought out Eleanor’s, and he gave her a look that was at once pleading and apologetic, before turning to make his greetings to his hostess. Eleanor watched as he then approached Catherine Croft. He bowed, and spoke to her in a voice too low for anyone else to hear. Whatever he said, it had the effect of bringing a faint flush of colour to her cheeks, though she did not look at him, keeping her eyes fixed on her lap. Mr. Harris looked from one to the other with a sort of placid incomprehension, as if a spaniel had interrupted his discussion of sheep-rot.

Dinner was announced, and Eleanor found herself seated between the vicar and Mr. Audley, with Catherine and Mr. Harris directly opposite. The situation was fraught with a tension that only a few at the table were aware of, which made the general conversation all the more absurd. The vicar spoke of parish matters; Mr. Harris spoke of crop rotation to Mr. Leigh, who listened with polite interest; and Mrs. Finch marvelled at the excellence of the boiled mutton.

I do hope you have not been unwell. You are looking a little pale, my love. We were all so diverted the other morning at your mother’s! Mr. Audley is such a wit, is he not? All that business about the book, and conjecturing! I declare, I did not understand half of it, but it was vastly amusing.”

Catherine’s pallor became ghastly. She stammered something about a headache, and looked with desperate appeal towards Eleanor, who immediately came to the rescue.

“Miss Leigh,” he said in a low, urgent tone. “May I have a word? I must speak with you.”

She glanced around the room. Her father was engaged with the vicar, and the others were occupied with the music. “Very well, Mr. Audley. But I must insist you are brief.”

When I first came here, I already knew something of Miss Croft’s situation. I did not know it all, but I knew of the existence of a… a secret understanding.”

Eleanor’s eyes widened. “You knew? And yet you tormented her so?”

“Pray, hear me out. The gentleman in question is a Mr. Davies. He is the younger brother of a dear friend of mine in London. He is a painter; a man of great talent and sensibility, but with no fortune and no prospects to speak of. He met Miss Croft last year when she was visiting her aunt in Bath. They formed a rapid and, I am told, a very powerful attachment. He has been her secret correspondent ever since.”

It all became clear to Eleanor in an instant. The book from a London bookseller; the intimate token of the music ribbon, taken from a piece she had played; the secrecy and the anxiety. It was the classic, unfortunate story.

“His brother, my friend, confided the matter to me,” Mr. Audley continued, his voice earnest. “He was concerned. Davies is impetuous, and the Crofts, he had heard, were intending their daughter for this Mr. Harris, a man of property. He asked me, as I was to be in this neighbourhood, to form a judgment of the young lady myself. To see if her character was as firm, and her affections as constant, as his brother believed.”

“And so you devised that cruel test,” Eleanor said, a fresh wave of indignation rising within her. “You decided to play with her, to see if she would break.”

“No,” he insisted, looking at her with painful sincerity. “That is, not in so cold-blooded a manner. I am not such a monster. I confess, my initial plan was simply to observe. But my own foolish nature, my love of a jest, got the better of me. When I saw the book, and guessed its origins, I could not resist the temptation to… to probe. I thought it a light-hearted mystery, a country-town intrigue. I imagined she might even be amused by my cleverness in discovering her. I had no conception, none at all, of the depth of her feeling, or the extremity of her situation with her family and with Mr. Harris. I did not know he was to be here this evening, pressing his suit. I did not know that every word I spoke was turning a knife in a genuine wound. I thought I was merely playing a part in a comedy. I did not realize it was a tragedy.”

He paused, and passed a hand over his eyes. “When I saw her face after I produced that wretched ribbon, I understood everything. I had not uncovered a flirtation; I had exposed a heart. My business in the next county was a fabrication. I rode to a posting-house and wrote a long letter to Davies, telling him what a fool I had been, and urging him to do something, to write to her family, to come down here himself, whatever the cost. For this state of affairs cannot continue. It is killing her.”

Eleanor looked across the room. Catherine had just finished playing. Mr. Harris was applauding loudly, and leaning in to speak to her with an air of smiling ownership. Catherine’s face was a mask of polite endurance. In that moment, Eleanor’s anger at Mr. Audley dissolved, replaced by a reluctant, complicated sympathy. He had indeed been a fool, a meddling, conceited fool, but his remorse was as profound as his error had been great. And he was, she now saw, trying to mend what he had broken.

“She ought not to be in this position,” Eleanor said, her voice softer. “Her parents should be told.”

“They should,” he agreed. “But she is afraid. She fears their disappointment, and she fears poverty, not for herself, but for him. She knows they would never consent to a match with a penniless artist when Mr. Harris and his three thousand a year are waiting for her.”

“Then she must choose,” Eleanor said simply.

“Yes,” he replied, his gaze returning to her. “She must. And I, by my profligate nonsense, have made that choice a matter of public urgency rather than private reflection. Can you, Miss Leigh, find it in your heart to forgive me? Not for my sake, but because I cannot be of any further use to her, or to him, if I do not have at least one ally in this place who understands the truth of the matter.”

Eleanor looked from his earnest, troubled face to the pale, composed one of Catherine Croft, and she knew that she could not refuse him. The affair had moved beyond the realm of amusement or judgment. It was now a matter of human unhappiness, and her own feelings of vexation seemed very small in comparison.

“I do not know if forgiveness is mine to give, Mr. Audley,” she said at last. “But I believe I understand. And if I can be of any service to Miss Croft, I will be.”

A look of immense relief washed over his features. “Thank you,” he said, so quietly she could barely hear him. “I knew I was not mistaken in you.” And as the party began to break up, and Mr. Harris moved to fetch Catherine’s shawl with the confident air of a man whose business is all but settled, Eleanor was left to conjecture, with a great deal more clarity and a great deal less peace of mind, on the very difficult part that a true and faithful friend might now be called upon to play.

Here, with the door closed and the house silent around them, Emma felt she could at last indulge in the luxury of her own superior understanding, and, in her benevolence, extend a little of its light to her companion.

“Now, Harriet,” she said, seating her by the window, “tell me what you truly thought of our little drama this morning.”

“Drama, Miss Woodhouse?” Harriet looked confused, as if she had missed some theatrical performance. “I thought it was all excessively pleasant.”

“Pleasant, yes; but was there nothing else that struck you? Nothing in the behaviour of any of the party that seemed, particular?”

Harriet’s brow furrowed in concentration. “Particular? Only that Mr. Churchill was so very kind, and so very amusing. And that Miss Fairfax looked so beautiful when she blushed. I do wonder who sent the pianoforte! Do you think it could really be Colonel Campbell?”

“Perhaps,” said Emma, smiling at her friend’s simplicity. “Or perhaps it is from someone who wishes to remain unknown for reasons of his own. It is a very interesting situation, Harriet, and requires a great deal of observation. One must look beyond what is said, to what is felt.”

She paused, arranging her thoughts for the most delicate and useful effect. She felt a tender pity for Harriet, who saw the world as a mere surface of pleasantries, and a corresponding sense of her own duty to furnish her with a little more depth.

“For instance,” she continued, her voice soft and confidential, “did you not perceive a certain melancholy in Mr. Knightley’s manner today?”

Harriet’s eyes widened. “Melancholy? No, indeed! I thought he was very, very much as he always is. He spoke so firmly to Miss Bates about Miss Fairfax.”

“Ah, but firmness may be a mask, Harriet. When a man of deep feeling is compelled by honour and circumstance to hide a tender partiality, he often adopts a manner of gruffness, or of excessive, brotherly concern. It is a disguise for a heart that is otherwise engaged.”

She watched Harriet’s face for a sign of comprehension, but saw only dutiful attentiveness. It was a little vexing, but also rather endearing. She had to draw the picture more clearly for her.

“A man like Mr. Knightley,” she went on, as if discussing a character in a novel, “a man of his standing and sense, does not bestow his affections lightly. And if he were to bestow them upon someone whose situation in life was far inferior to his own, and for whom there might be other attachments, or at least, the suspicion of other attachments, do you not think it would cause him a great deal of private suffering? He would be too honourable to declare himself, and too much in love to be easy.”

Harriet looked quite alarmed. “In love? Mr. Knightley? Oh, Miss Woodhouse, who do you mean? Is he very unhappy?”

“I only conjecture, of course,” said Emma, retreating into intellectual modesty, now that her point was made. “It is merely an idea of my own. But I believe he is not a man whose heart is at liberty. And it would be a great pity, would it not, for any young woman to fancy herself the object of his attention, when his affections are already secretly bestowed elsewhere?”

The implication was as plain as Emma dared to make it. She had, with this one charitable speech, protected Harriet from the folly of ever raising her eyes to Mr. Knightley, a danger which, though remote, was always possible, and had done so by means of her own brilliant deduction concerning Jane Fairfax. It was killing two birds with one stone, an exercise in both friendship and sagacity.

Harriet sighed. “I suppose it would. Poor Mr. Knightley. To be unhappy! I cannot bear to think of it. He has always been so very good to me.”

Emma was satisfied. The seed was planted. Harriet would now view Mr. Knightley through a lens of respectful pity, as a man whose destiny was fixed. His attentions would be interpreted as mere kindness, his criticisms as the gruffness of a man with a secret sorrow. The field was cleared. Her satisfaction in her own management was immense. She had not only solved a riddle, but had used the solution for the betterment of her friend. What could be more complete?

The next few days passed quietly. Frank Churchill had returned to Enscombe, and Highbury settled back into its accustomed rhythms. The pianoforte at the Bateses’ was an established fact, though its origins remained a subject of tireless speculation for Miss Bates, and of knowing silence for Jane Fairfax. Emma, for her part, found her conviction regarding Mr. Knightley a source of constant, quiet amusement. Every time she saw him, she looked for fresh evidence, and was never disappointed. A thoughtful expression, a moment of abstraction, a particular gravity when Jane Fairfax’s name was mentioned, all were noted and added to her collection of proofs.

About a week after the visit to the Bateses’, Mrs. Weston called at Hartfield. She came alone, and Emma surmised that she wished for a private conversation, a wish that was always flattering. Mr. Woodhouse having been settled for his afternoon nap, the two ladies had the drawing-room to themselves.

“My dear Emma,” Mrs. Weston began, taking her hand, “I have been wanting to see you. I have had a letter from Frank.”

“Indeed!” said Emma, her interest immediately piqued. “I hope he is well, and that Mrs. Churchill’s health is no worse.”

“She is much as she always is, which is to say, very demanding,” Mrs. Weston said with a slight smile. “But Frank writes in very good spirits. He was excessively pleased with his visit, and particularly with his reception here at Hartfield. He speaks of you a great deal, Emma.”

“Does he?” Emma contrived to look merely politely interested. “I am glad we were able to make his stay in Highbury agreeable.”

“Agreeable! He calls it delightful. He charged me to say a thousand things to you. He was quite captivated, my dear Emma. I have never known him so taken with anyone.”

This was very welcome intelligence; it accorded perfectly with Emma’s own observations. She had seen Frank Churchill’s admiration in his every look and word. It was only natural.

Mrs. Weston continued, a little more earnestly. “You know, Emma, it is the fondest wish of his father’s heart, and of mine, to see him happily married. And I confess, since I have seen you and him together, I have allowed myself to form a little hope.”

Emma laughed. “You are a dreadful matchmaker, my dear Mrs. Weston. Worse than I am! We must not run ahead of ourselves. Mr. Frank Churchill and I have been acquainted for a very short time.”

“A short time, perhaps, but some people do not need a great deal of time to understand one another. He found in you a quickness of mind and a vivacity of spirit that he has not met with elsewhere.”

“He is very obliging,” Emma replied, her composure unruffled. She was in no hurry. The idea of Frank Churchill was a pleasant one, but the certainty of his admiration was, for the moment, pleasure enough.

Their conversation was so agreeably personal that Emma was surprised when Mrs. Weston shifted the topic. “But it was not only of Frank I wished to speak. I have been thinking of our conversation the other morning, at Mrs. Bates’s, and something you said has been puzzling me ever since.”

“Has it?”

“Yes. It was your fancy, for you must allow it to be a fancy, about Mr. Knightley.”

Emma’s smile became a little more fixed. “Ah, yes. My conjecture. You thought me very foolish, I dare say.”

“Not foolish, my dear, never foolish. But mistaken. I am sure you are mistaken. Mr. Knightley and Jane Fairfax! The more I consider it, the more impossible it seems. I have known him since he was a boy, Emma. His regard for her is exactly that which he holds for you and your sister: one of old family connexion and long-standing friendship. There is nothing of romance in it.”

Emma felt the pleasant challenge of defending a superior opinion against a well-meaning, but less perceptive, friend. It was a position she enjoyed.

“You may be right, of course,” she said, with an air of generous concession. “You have indeed known him a great while. And yet, Mrs. Weston, are not the deepest feelings often the best concealed? Especially from those who have always seen one in a certain light? They would not look for a change, and so they would not perceive it.”

“But what change is there to perceive? What did you see, Emma, that has so convinced you?”

Here was her moment. She leaned forward, her eyes bright with the pleasure of her own narrative. “I saw a man ill at ease. When Frank Churchill was teasing Miss Fairfax, a teasing I admit I encouraged a little, Mr. Knightley’s countenance was one of decided displeasure. Not the general displeasure of a man who dislikes nonsense, but a specific, personal vexation. Then, his arrival at the Bateses’, so immediately after!, and his enquiries, which were all for her. ‘How is Miss Fairfax?’ he asked, over and over. He would not be put off. It was the anxiety of a lover, not a mere neighbour.”

Mrs. Weston looked thoughtful, but unconvinced. “It was the anxiety of a very kind-hearted man, Emma, who had just seen a girl of delicate health undergo a great deal of agitation. You know how he is. He was just as anxious when your father had that little cold last autumn.”

“But it was the manner of it!” Emma insisted. “And there was more. When I spoke to him afterwards at our own door, and mentioned his coming to her defence, he coloured. Mr. Knightley! A man who is never at a loss, never embarrassed. He coloured quite distinctly. And his final words to me, a warning not to let my ‘fancy run away with me.’ What could that mean, but a fear that I, with my active mind, might guess his secret?”

She sat back, triumphant. The evidence, when laid out so, seemed to her irrefutable. She had built a case as solid as Donwell Abbey itself.

Mrs. Weston shook her head slowly, a gentle smile on her lips. “My dear, clever Emma. You build a very pretty story. But I believe you are reading the book upside down. Could his vexation not have been on your account? Perhaps he dislikes seeing you engaged in a flirtation with Frank Churchill, whom he does not yet know well, and whose attentions might be frivolous. And could his warning about fancy not be a general caution to you, as he has so often cautioned you before, not to meddle and imagine things?”

Emma experienced a flash of impatience. Mrs. Weston was twisting everything. To imagine Mr. Knightley’s concern was for her, Emma Woodhouse, was to revert to the old, dull, brotherly footing she had just succeeded in making so much more interesting.

“I think not,” she said coolly. “Mr. Knightley knows I am perfectly capable of judging Mr. Churchill for myself. No, his feelings on that score are of a different nature altogether. He sees a rival. As for his cautions, they have always been about my matchmaking. This was different. It was personal. It was a plea.”

She saw that she could not persuade her friend. Mrs. Weston’s mind was too habituated to its old tracks to follow Emma’s nimbler diversions. It was a pity; but it did not in the least shake Emma’s own confidence. It rather enhanced it. To see what others could not, that was the true mark of penetration. Mrs. Weston saw the surface; she, Emma, had plumbed the depths.

“Well,” said Mrs. Weston, seeing it was fruitless to argue. “We shall see. Time will tell which of us is the better prophet. For my part, I shall continue to put my faith in Frank Churchill’s attentions to you, and leave Mr. Knightley to his strawberry beds.”

The conversation turned again to lighter matters, but Emma felt a new security in her opinion. It had been tested against the good sense of Mrs. Weston and had not yielded an inch. She felt a great tenderness for Mr. Knightley, and a great amusement at the world’s blindness. She and he were the only two people in Highbury, it seemed, who understood the true state of his heart; and he, poor man, did not know that she shared his secret. The knowledge gave her a feeling of power that was exquisitely pleasant; a secret directorship in the drama of Highbury society. She looked forward with relish to the next act.
